attempts.raw_response: "Perhaps it is one of those things that no man can decide for another, but which each must settle for himself, as best he may, according to his own strength and weakness. For my own part, I have seen both happen. I have known men who were saved by a good wife from ruin and dissipation, who became honest and industrious, who found in the love of a virtuous woman something to live for beyond the mere gratification of their appetites. And I have known others who were dragged down by wives who were wasteful or wicked, or who simply had no sympathy with their husband's better nature. The truth is, the choice of a companion for life is the most important any man can make, and yet it is a lottery."

But if I were not a
commissioned officer of the United States, and a thing of Rules and
Regulations who can dance and wear a uniform, and a youth generally
unfit to pose as an example, I would advise you not to sign this, but
to go home and brace up and leave whiskey alone.

"Now, what shall we do?" said the young lieutenant, smiling; "shall we
tear this up, or will you sign it?"

The applicant's lips were twitching as well as his hands now, and he
rubbed his cuff over his face and smiled back.

"I'm much obliged to you," he said, nervously. "That sounds a rather
flat thing to say, I know, but if you knew all I meant by it, though,
it would mean enough.

"And, on the other hand, it may be that there are some good women who
could keep you on shore, and help you to do something more with
yourself than to carry a musket. And, again, it may be that if you
stayed on shore you would drink yourself more or less comfortably to
death, and break somebody's heart. I can't tell.

source_document.title: Van Bibber and Others by Richard Harding Davis
